items.title: Academic publishers must not get stuck in 'war of AI against AI', STM chief exec warns
items.excerpt: STM chief executive Caroline Sutton warns that academic publishers risk an escalating machine-vs-machine arms race as AI-fabricated submissions meet AI screening tools. She argues automated integrity checks must stay paired with human editorial judgement rather than replace it.

items.title: Spotify Adds More AI-Powered Discovery Tools for Audiobooks
items.excerpt: Spotify is testing three new AI-driven audiobook features: an automated playlist generator, natural-language catalogue search and smarter series tracking. The move pushes book discovery further away from category browsing and toward conversational, model-driven recommendation.

items.title: What Authors Expect Now, and Why Publishing Hasn't Kept Up: An Interview with Jennifer Fleet and Christian Grubak
items.excerpt: Aries Systems and ChronosHub are wiring submission systems together to fix a manuscript workflow authors still find punishing. The interview digs into automated taxonomy matching, AI manuscript triage, and why clean structured data is the precondition for any useful LLM layer in publishing.

items.title: Seven-figure book deal canceled; Hugh Howey says it's the "end of an era"
items.excerpt: A debut novelist's $2m+ deal collapsed after his own agents concluded the manuscript was substantially AI-assisted, with no reliable detector involved in the call. Hugh Howey reads it as the end of an era in which a polished manuscript alone could be trusted as evidence of authorship.

items.title: 'It was inevitable': Agents react to major book deal that collapsed over suspected AI use
items.excerpt: A crime novel that sold for $2.4m in a 14-way US auction was withdrawn by its agent on 31 July over suspected AI use. Agents told The Bookseller the collapse was predictable, with uncertainty and fear now the dominant mood in acquisitions.

items.title: 'Genius' novel sold in six- and seven-figure deals at auction pulled over AI allegations
items.excerpt: The breaking report on the crime novel pulled from both US and UK publication after allegations of AI involvement in its creation. It is the first time a headline auction title has been withdrawn mid-deal on authorship grounds.

items.title: Legal Battle Over U.S. Copyright Chief Heats Up Again
items.excerpt: The fight over whether the president can remove Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter is back in court, and it turns on AI. Her attempted removal followed the Copyright Office report concluding that training models on copyrighted works can exceed fair use — the finding that underpins authors' leverage in every current AI suit.

items.title: Around the Book World: August 3, 2026
items.excerpt: The weekly international roundup notes Korean readers leaning on generative AI for recommendations — to the point that one reader says people 'are using AI so much that they're losing time to read.' It also tallies Hachette's expected $22m+ payout from the Anthropic settlement across roughly 15,000 titles.

items.title: How Substack's AI Detector Puts Authors at Risk | Self-Publishing News (July 30th, 2026)
items.excerpt: Dale L. Roberts walks indie authors through Substack's Pangram-powered AI detection rollout and the false-positive exposure it creates for writers. The weekly news episode frames detection as the new gatekeeping layer authors have to publish around.

items.title: Study Claims Viral Bestseller DAGGERMOUTH is AI-Generated
items.excerpt: A Stony Brook study run through the Pangram detector estimates one in five Kindle ebooks now contain more than 25% AI-generated text, and flags BookTok hit Daggermouth at roughly 60%. The author denies the claim, sharpening the question of whether detector scores can ever be treated as evidence.

items.title: Researchers attempt to prove that generative AI dilutes the market for books
items.excerpt: Academics are building the empirical case that AI-generated titles measurably harm the market for human-written books — the missing evidence in most fair-use arguments. Friedman argues authors angry about AI training should welcome the attempt to quantify market harm rather than assert it.

items.title: The Published Voice: Whose Voice Are We Really Reading?
items.excerpt: Drawing on an EASE panel called 'Beyond Track Changes,' Roohi Ghosh asks what is left of an author's voice once AI-driven editing smooths every manuscript toward the same 'native' register. The piece treats voice as a craft asset that automated editing quietly erodes, and argues editors have to measure their impact on it rather than assume it survives.

items.title: "Avoiding AI" Library Programs, and More Updates For Library Workers
items.excerpt: Public libraries are now running patron workshops on how to opt out of AI — search, assistants, and the defaults baked into everyday software. Book Riot's library-worker roundup treats 'avoiding AI' as a teachable literacy skill, a counter-programming move against the assumption that every reading and research tool should be model-mediated.

items.title: These new features are coming to the iFlytek AINOTE 2
items.excerpt: iFlytek published a 2026 roadmap for its LLM-powered E-Ink tablet, layering AI meeting transcription, automated note organization and document processing on top of a reworked handwriting and PDF toolbar. It is a concrete look at what an AI-native reading-and-writing device wants to become once the model sits underneath the page.

items.title: Princeton University Press Partners with Cashmere on AI Licensing
items.excerpt: Princeton University Press will make its catalogue available to 'copyright compliant' AI platforms through Cashmere, a licensing intermediary built for retrieval-augmented generation rather than model training. The press keeps title-by-title control over what is licensed and on what terms — an early template for how books get into AI answers without being swallowed into weights.

items.title: AI May Be Making Publishing Easier, But It's Still Not Easy
items.excerpt: At the Media Transformation Summit, publishers reported that AI has genuinely lowered production cost — audiobooks especially — while leaving the hard parts untouched: deciding what to publish and finding readers. The recurring practical lesson was that machine-readable metadata and management buy-in, not the model itself, decide whether an AI workflow lands.
